newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Netanyahu sees Israel as Silicon Valley of East.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu sees Israel as Silicon Valley of East.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, painting a glowing picture of Israel's potential, told an elite group of government and business leaders on Sunday that his country could become the Silicon Valley of the East.

"Israel is undergoing an enormous revolution. It is one of only three or four countries in the world being rapidly catapulted into a hub of high technology," he said in a speech to the World Economic Forum.
The country was "fast becoming not just the Silicon Valley of the Middle East but the Silicon Valley of the whole Eastern Hemisphere," he added.

Stressing that prosperity was one of the key principles on which lasting peace in the Middle East had to be built, the right-wing premier said that Israel had the ability to double its $17,000 per capita income within the next decade.

This well-being could bring benefits well beyond Israel's borders, creating jobs for Palestinian workers and leading to partnerships in high-tech ventures with Arab countries, particularly Egypt, he said.
"The idea of a high-tech Israel and low-tech neighbours would be destabilising," the Israeli leader added.

Netanyahu, who met Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak at Davos, which stages an annual get-together of political and business leaders, said that Israel had unique advantages in an increasingly technology-dominated world.

The country had the world's highest per capita concentration of scientists, many of whom formed part of the brain drain from former Soviet Bloc before and after the collapse of the Communist regimes of Eastern Europe.
"Ours is a knowledge-based economy," he said.
Israel's powerful military-industrial complex, built up over the years of open or simmering conflict with its Arab neighours, was increasingly being put to civilian uses, he said.
Unlike many European countries, Israel was also not encumbered with a significant amount of heavy industry which needed modernising. "We have no dinosaurs, no industrial baggage," he said.
But Netanyahu, who took office in June this year, said that work still needed to be done on knocking Israel's state finances into shape and to introduce greater competition into its financial system.
Noting that 80 percent of the banking industry was controlled by just three institutions, he said that the government intended to break up this excessive concentration.
